title: The Philosophy of Breaking People Down Before Building Them Up
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece traces the military 'tear down to build up' training philosophy and argues the evidence now contradicts it: coercive environments reduce creativity, impair learning, and stifle decision-making even as they build group bonding through shared hardship. Most military academies have shifted toward support, mentoring, and trust in the last two decades, but the author notes corporate and athletic teams still emulate the harsher original version through extreme hours, sink-or-swim onboarding, and pay-your-dues traditions. The piece closes by insisting fear and coercion are not required for excellence, calling for the tear-down philosophy itself to be retired.
points: Coercive 'tear down' training increases group bonding through shared hardship but reduces creativity, candor, learning, and decision-making quality.
Most military academies have already shifted toward support, mentoring, and trust over the last two decades.
Corporate and athletic teams still often emulate the harsher, outdated version through extreme hours and sink-or-swim onboarding.
The best leaders, including those from military backgrounds, now pair high standards with psychological safety and authority with humility.
quotes: Military academies describe the process as “tearing down to build up.

While shared hardship increases group bonding, coercive environments, like those found in the military during the tear-down phase, have been shown to reduce creativity, impede candid communication, impair learning, and stifle sound decision-making.
So, despite centuries-old traditions, most military education over the last two decades has shifted toward more support, mentoring, and trust during the initial phase.

Over the years, corporations have developed traditions of extreme hours, sink-or-swim onboarding, internal team member competition, pressure testing under uncertainty, and a “pay your dues” mentality — all echoing the tear-down philosophy.
Decades of research now paint an unequivocal picture: Fear, coercion, and breakdown are not necessary to create personal or team excellence.
